body:
[aida:product] PRIORITY OVER MY QUEUE ORDER: #2058 FIXES A WINDOWS BUILD BREAK THAT LANDED ON MAIN TONIGHT, AND IT CAME IN THROUGH MY OWN MERGED PR.

WHAT IS BROKEN. #2040 (BUG-1454), which you merged, carries a test opening with a bare `use std::os::unix::fs::PermissionsExt;`. std::os::unix does not exist on a Windows target, so this is a COMPILE error, not a failing test - it takes the whole aida-cli-lib test target with it and every other test on that leg stops reporting. The import was in the codex author's original test; I edited that test in rework and did not catch it, so treat it as mine.

I VERIFIED IT RATHER THAN REASONING FROM THE RULE, because the repo's own guard cannot answer the question: `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` dies in ring's build script, exactly the foreign-C-dependency limitation CLAUDE.md documents. So I compiled a file containing only that import:

    x86_64-pc-windows-msvc    error[E0433]: could not find `unix` in `os`
    x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu  compiles clean

and then compiled the FIXED form the same way - clean on both. Two targets, same file, Linux as the control in each direction.

ONE INSTANCE, AND I WANT TO FLAG HOW I NEARLY MISREPORTED IT. My first sweep grepped for ungated std::os::unix and returned FOURTEEN hits across the workspace. That number is wrong and I almost sent it to you. Windows compiled this crate successfully at 84a7ea68a0 with 5194 tests running, so everything present at that commit is gated somewhere my six-line lookback window could not see. The correct instrument was diffing 84a7ea68a0..main: three unix usages added since the last known-green Windows run, two of them already carrying #[cfg(unix)], one not. That one is the break.

This is the same failure mode you warned me about this morning in a different costume - a measurement taken with the wrong instrument, offered with a confident count attached. The difference is only that I checked it before sending.

THE FIX HAS TWO HALVES and both are needed: #[cfg(unix)] around the chmod block so the Windows target COMPILES, and #[cfg_attr(windows, ignore = ...)] because a shebang fake gh is not executable there. An ignored test still has to compile, so the attribute alone would not have done it. The STORY-1043 detector test already uses exactly this pairing.

BUG-1565 filed and approved; #2058 is the PR.

FOR BUG-1556's EVIDENCE, not to argue here: all three documented PR-time guards were present and none could see this. PR CI is Linux-only by design; the portability ratchet greps Rust test code for path and shell assumptions but has no rule for a cfg-less std::os::unix import; the report-only Windows target check cannot run to completion on this workspace. It was caught only because I was reading a cross-platform run on an unrelated PR head for a different reason. That is a fourth guard-gap instance to add to that spec's classification work, and it is a CHEAP one to close - a ratchet rule for cfg-less std::os::* in test code would have caught it at PR time.

WHERE I AM OTHERWISE: #2035 (BUG-1470) pushed at 70a11d23b4 and mergeable - advisor gate at the flip, corrected --help table with verbatim_doc_comment (the table was being reflowed into mush, and so was the three-command block above it, which is a pre-existing defect that fix also repairs), pass-through test coverage, and F4 dispositioned as BUG-1564 / TASK-1423 / STORY-1429 so the merge closes only criterion 1.

#2030 (BUG-1485) is in progress. F1 turned out small: phase 3 ALREADY has the worktree-free recovery helper (try_open_orchestrator_pr_for_no_pr_pushed_branch, BUG-895), and phase 1 simply never used it. `ahead == 0` was conflating "looked and found nothing" with "could not look because the worktree is gone" - unwrap_or(0) flattening a None. Phase 1 now falls back to the existing helper rather than getting new recovery logic. F2 (extend the fixture past branch recovery to assert the PR outcome) is what I am on now.
subject: MERGE #2058 AHEAD OF MY QUEUE: Windows BUILD BREAK landed via #2040 (my miss) — verified two-target, one instance
